title: ropeway:handbook-title-52
text: A ropeway is a machine on your mechanical network, like a quern or a helve hammer. The drive turns the haul rope, the haul rope pulls the cabin, and the cabin runs at whatever speed the network is turning. Nothing is stored and nothing is banked: a bigger drive is a faster cabin, and no drive is a cabin that waits. Building the drive 1. Build a drive housing within eight blocks of any tower on the line. It is the machine that turns the haul rope, and a line with none anywhere on it has no drive and will not move. A housing answers to the single nearest footing that is already part of a line and turns that line and no other, so if two lines run close together, stand the housing plainly nearer the one it is meant to drive. A lone footing dropped to mark out the next tower is not a line yet and is skipped, however close it stands - but two old footings still linked to each other are a line, and one of those nearer than yours will take the housing off it. Those eight blocks are measured straight through the air, so height counts the same as distance across the ground: the housing may stand on the ground beside the footing, or up level with a windmill's axle, whichever the mill needs. 2. Run an axle into it from a windmill or a water wheel. It takes power on any of its four sides - four horizontal faces, never its roof - so the last stretch of the run is always level. Put the housing at the height of the mill's own axle and that is the whole of it: two or three wooden axles, straight and level, no angled gears. 3. Build one tension weight within eight blocks of any tower on the line. It keeps the haul rope taut, and a line will not carry a cabin until it has one. It is not a machine: nothing winds it, it holds no charge and it takes no axle. A windmill needs room, and the room decides the height A rotor turns in a flat disc one block thick, standing square to its own axle, and the game will not let you add a sail unless that disc is clear: one clear block for every sail, and one more, counted upward and sideways exactly as much as downward. Nothing behind the rotor along its axle is ever checked, which is why a mill bolts happily to the side of a tower and why the axle run coming out of it never blocks the mill it serves. So a rotor low enough to stand beside a housing on the ground refuses its first sail. Three sails want four clear blocks under the hub; a maxed five-sail wooden rotor wants six. Count the clear blocks rather than a height - the room is what the game checks, and a height is one out or not depending on whether you counted from the grass or from the block resting on it. It is a count of blocks and not of altitude, so a trench under the disc does as well as air: half the clearance can be dug rather than built. Build the housing up beside the hub at the same height and the run stays two or three level axles - a housing six blocks above the footing block still measures inside the eight, with five blocks of sideways room to spare. And it needs open sky. A rotor that cannot see daylight makes no torque at all, however hard the wind blows and however clear its disc: the game reads the sky light at the hub, and a mill under a roof, a canopy or an overhanging shelf of rock reads dark and simply stands still. That is about cover and not about the hour - a mill in the open turns all night. It is the last remaining way to build the whole drive correctly and get nothing out of it, so if the disc is clear and the weather is good, look up. The maxed metal rotor is the exception. Ten sails need eleven clear blocks every way, which stands that hub eleven blocks above the footing beside it - and eleven blocks of height alone is already outside the eight, wherever you put the housing. That drive has to come down a column: an angled gear at the hub, three vertical wooden axles, a second angled gear beside a housing seven blocks above the footing. Five vanilla blocks, and the second gear is there because the housing takes an axle on its sides and not on its roof. Give the vertical axles a wall to lean on, or the gear beside them refuses to place. The bullwheel is a marker, not a machine You may swap any tower's pylon head for a bullwheel. It costs the tower nothing - a drive tower is the same sixteen blocks as any other - and it changes nothing mechanical: it takes no axle and is on no network. What it does is turn, at the speed your drive is turning, and stop when your drive stops. Put one on the tower nearest your mill and you can tell from across the valley whether the line is running. A bigger mill is a faster cabin Hauling a cabin is a heavy load - about three querns' worth - and the line's speed is what your drive has left over after carrying it. In good wind, on the level: Two sails - a wooden rotor with two sails will not shift the cabin at all. Three sails - about 1.2 blocks a second, a walking pace. Five sails, a maxed wooden rotor - about 2.2. Ten sails, a maxed metal rotor - about 3.0, a run. Where the mill stands matters as much as how big it is Those speeds are good wind, and good wind is the top of the range rather than the middle of it. Wind also strengthens with height. The same maxed wooden rotor that barely creeps the cabin along - a third of a block a second - down at sea level in ordinary weather will run it at over 1.6 from a ridge eighty blocks up, and a three-sail mill in the valley will often not move it at all. Put the drive high. A ropeway is a mountain machine, and so is the mill that drives it. Water wheels A water wheel does not care what the weather is doing, and it is the one drive that hooks up on the ground with nothing to climb: power comes out of both ends of its own axle, at most a block above the water surface, so a housing standing on the bank at that height takes a short level axle run and nothing else. It asks for everything up front instead. A wheel only turns in rapidly flowing water - the white water that generates, rarely, in high mountain streams, and that no player can place or make. Ordinary river water will not move it, however deep or fast it looks. The wheel is iron-age as well: two four-way hubs on an axle to craft the block, and then six stages of construction on the spot in support beams, planks, resin and nails. And it is capped lower than a windmill - whatever the river does, a water wheel cannot run the cabin past about 1.8 blocks a second. Constant, capped and built where the map allows, against faster but at the mercy of the wind and the altitude: that is the whole choice. Gearing and anything else on a vanilla network behave as they do everywhere else. You never have to guess: the drive housing's block info panel reads out what it is turning at, and any footing's reads what the line comes to in blocks a second. Power may enter anywhere, and drives add up There is no designated drive station. Put the housing where the terrain suits it - wind on a ridge, water in the valley - beside whichever tower of your line is nearest that spot, and if one mill is not enough, build a second housing beside another tower of the same line on its own axle network. Their speeds pool, so two mills is a visibly faster cabin. It has to be a second network, mind: two housings tapped off the one axle run are the same drive twice over, and they are worse than one - the line reads that drive's speed once, but each housing puts the full haul load on that network, so the cabin ends up slower. And it is only ever one line: a housing pitched between two of them is not shared, it turns whichever of them has the nearer footing and the other reports no drive at all, however close its towers stand. Intermediate drive stations were real on long ropeways for exactly this reason: driving the haul loop anywhere along its length drives all of it. Climbing costs A climbing cabin is a heavier load than a level one, so the same mill turns slower while it climbs and picks up again on the flat. On a steep line a small mill crawls. That is the machine working rather than a fault - and it is the honest reason to put a bigger rotor on a mountain line. Dead calm Vanilla weather goes still for hours at a time and no windmill of any size makes torque then. The cabin stops where it is and waits, exactly like a quern with nobody turning it, and sets off again by itself when the wind returns. A stopped cabin is not a locked one - but mind where it stopped. Sneak steps you straight out of it wherever it happens to be, and if that is halfway across a span, you step out into the air and take the fall. Ride it out, or pick your moment. A cabin that is moving refuses that same key press until you hold it down - see Building a Line. If you would rather not wait on the weather, drive the line with something that does not depend on it, or build a second drive somewhere the wind reaches when the first one's does not.
